title: Linked lists

story.title: A treasure hunt for your friends
story.summary: You set up a treasure hunt. Each clue says where the next clue is hidden, so adding, dropping and rearranging stops has to stay easy however long the hunt gets.

uses.title: Hash map collision chains
uses.body: When two keys land in the same bucket, the bucket keeps them as a short linked list. You meet this in the Hash maps Lesson.

uses.title: LRU cache in front of a database
uses.body: A hash map finds an entry and a doubly linked list orders entries by recent use, so touching one relinks a few nodes.

uses.title: Kernel lists of processes and timers
uses.body: The OS kernel threads its process and timer records into linked lists through the records themselves, so adding or removing one relinks only its neighbours.

uses.title: Memory allocator free lists
uses.body: An allocator links its free blocks into a list, so handing out or taking back a block changes only a few links.

whenNot: Arrays usually win for indexed reads and for visiting every item. Their items sit side by side in memory, so the CPU cache loads many at once and index lookup is O(1). Choose a linked list when you often insert or remove in the middle at a node you already hold, plus the node before it for removals.

outcomes.explain-nodes-and-links: Explain how nodes and links make up a linked list
outcomes.traverse-from-head: Traverse a linked list from its head with a pointer

outcomes.delete-by-relinking: Delete a node by relinking around it

overview.title: A chain where each item knows the next
overview.caption: A [[linked-list]] is a chain of items where each item knows only where the next one is. A treasure hunt works the same way: each clue says where the next clue is hidden, you hand out the first clue, and the last clue says the treasure is here. You use a chain like this when you keep adding and removing items in the middle.

the-problem.title: A new stop means renumbering the sheet
the-problem.caption: You write your clues in numbered order on one sheet, like an array. Now you add a new stop, Clock, after clue 2. Every clue behind it, Oven and Shed here, moves one place down and gets a new number. The longer the hunt, the more you renumber for every new stop. You want adding a stop not to depend on how long the hunt is.
the-problem.keyIdea: Inserting in the middle of an array shifts every item behind it.

a-clue.title: A clue becomes a node
a-clue.caption: You write each clue on its own card and hide it under its own spot. A [[node]] holds two things: the spot it is hidden at and a link called `next`, where to look for the following clue. Here the node holds Mat, and its `next` points nowhere yet.
a-clue.keyIdea: Clues can be hidden anywhere; only the links give them an order.

chaining-clues.title: Clues chained into a hunt
chaining-clues.caption: You add Mail, Oven and Shed, then make each clue point at the one after it. Following the links takes you from Mat to Shed. The last clue's `next` is `null`, which marks the end of the chain: the treasure is there.

the-first-clue.title: The head is the clue you hand out
the-first-clue.caption: The hunt needs one more thing: the [[head]], a reference to its first clue. You set the head to Mat, the one clue no other clue points to, and hand it to your friends. From the head, the links reach every other clue.

finger-on-a-clue.title: A pointer marks the clue being read
finger-on-a-clue.caption: A [[pointer]] is a labelled marker that refers to one node. You place `here` on Mat, the clue being read right now. When the clue is solved, the marker moves along its `next` link.

following-the-trail.title: Following the trail
following-the-trail.caption: To check the whole hunt, you follow it. `here` starts on Mat and follows `next` to Mail, Oven and Shed. Shed's `next` is `null`, so the trail ends. Visiting the nodes one after another like this is [[traversal]].

add-a-stop.title: A new stop rewrites two clues
add-a-stop.caption: You stand at Mail and write a new clue, Clock. First its `next` points to Oven, the stop that follows it. Only then do you rewrite Mail's `next` to point to Clock. Two links change and no clue moves, so the cost does not depend on the length of the hunt.
add-a-stop.keyIdea: Point the new node forward first, then rewrite the old node to reach it.

remove-a-stop.title: Skip a stop by rewriting the clue before it
remove-a-stop.caption: Oven turns out too hard, so you drop it. You point `prev` at Clock, the clue before it, and rewrite Clock's `next` to Shed. Nothing points at Oven any more, so you remove it. The other clues never move.
remove-a-stop.keyIdea: To remove a node, rewrite the node before it to skip it.

jump-to-a-clue.title: Jumping to a clue takes a walk
jump-to-a-clue.caption: A chain of clues has no numbers to jump by. To reach index 3, which holds Shed, you start at the first clue, index 0, and follow `next` three times. Clue 50 sits at index 49, so reaching it takes 49 links. Reaching index `k` takes `k` moves.
jump-to-a-clue.keyIdea: A linked list has no index: reaching position `k` means following `k` links.

sheet-vs-trail.title: The sheet and the trail side by side
sheet-vs-trail.caption: The sheet reaches Shed in one jump by number, while the trail follows three links. The trail adds a stop by changing two links, while the sheet shifts every clue behind it. Reading out every clue visits each one once on both.
sheet-vs-trail.keyIdea: Pick the structure by the operation you repeat most.

reverse-preview.title: Next up: run the hunt backwards
reverse-preview.caption: In Practice you lay the trail backwards, so the hunt ends where it began: the last clue becomes the first, by reversing the list in place. You use three pointers: `prev`, `current` and `next`. Before the first move, `prev` is `null`, `current` sits on the head and `next` is one node ahead. You redirect each clue's link, one at a time.

where-you-meet-it.title: Where you will meet it
where-you-meet-it.caption: Here is where you meet linked lists outside this hunt. Each keeps items in order and changes them at a spot it already holds. The note under them says when an array is the better pick.

what-a-clue-holds.prompt: Mat is a single clue, and a next clue, Mail, will follow it. What must the Mat clue hold besides its own spot?

options.next-link: A link to the next clue, because the hunt continues by following it
options.copy-of-next: A copy of the next clue's text, because then you can read the next clue without going there
options.position-number: Its number on the sheet, because the hunt finds each clue by its number
options.nothing-extra: Nothing more, because the clues lie side by side like boxes on the sheet

what-a-clue-holds.explanation: The Mat clue holds a link to the next clue, called `next`, and the hunt continues by following it. A copy of Mail's text says nothing about where Mail is hidden, and it goes stale if you rewrite that clue. Clues have no number, because a list finds a clue by following the links. Clues do not lie side by side in memory, so without a link nothing connects Mat to Mail.

which-clue-is-first.prompt: The hunt has no head yet. Select the clue the head should refer to.
which-clue-is-first.explanation: The head is Mat, because no link leads into Mat, so only the head can lead you there. If the head referred to Oven, you would lose Mat and Mail. If it referred to Shed, the last clue, you could reach nothing else, since its `next` is `null`.

where-the-walk-lands.prompt: `here` starts on Mat and follows `next` one link at a time. After two moves, which clue is it on?
where-the-walk-lands.explanation: It is on Oven: the first move reaches Mail and the second reaches Oven. It does not stop on Mail, because a move counts only when you follow a link. It does not reach Shed either, since that takes a third move. Links only point forward, so `here` never goes back.

first-rewrite-for-new-stop.prompt: A new clue, Clock, is about to join the hunt right after Mail. Which link do you set first?

options.new-to-next: Clock's `next`, set to Oven, because Clock must lead to the stop after it before anything points at Clock
options.previous-to-new: Mail's `next`, set to Clock, because the clue before the new stop must lead to it
options.new-to-previous: Clock's `next`, set to Mail, because Clock should point back at the stop before it
options.either-order: Either one first, because both links are set in the end

first-rewrite-for-new-stop.explanation: You set Clock's `next` to Oven first, because Clock must lead to the stop that follows it. If you point it at Mail instead, Mail then points to Clock and Clock back to Mail, so the hunt loops and Oven and Shed become unreachable. If you point Mail at Clock first, nothing points to Oven any more and the rest of the hunt is lost. The order matters because Mail's old `next` is the only reference to the rest of the trail.

clue-before-the-removed.prompt: You drop Oven from the hunt. Select the clue whose `next` link must change.
clue-before-the-removed.explanation: Clock's `next` must change, because Clock is the clue that points at Oven. Mail's `next` already points at Clock and stays as it is. Shed is the last clue and has no `next` to follow. You point Clock straight at Shed, and Oven drops out.

cost-of-reaching-clue-k.prompt: A friend asks for the clue at index `k`, where the first clue is index 0. How much work does it take to reach it, counting from the first clue?

options.k-moves: `k` moves, because you follow `k` links from the first clue: O(n) at worst
options.one-move: 1 move, because the hunt knows where each clue is: O(1)
options.whole-trail: n moves, because you always follow the whole trail: O(n)
options.halving: About log `k` moves, because you can skip clues along the way

cost-of-reaching-clue-k.explanation: You follow `k` links from the first clue, so the cost grows with `k` and is O(n) in the worst case. A list cannot jump the way an array does, because clues are not stored side by side. The walk stops at index `k` rather than at the end. A link only leads to the next clue, so there is nothing to skip.

cheaper-on-a-trail.prompt: Imagine the same hunt written on one numbered sheet instead. Which job is cheaper with chained clues than with the sheet?

options.insert-after-current: Adding a stop right after a clue you hold, because only two links change and no clue moves
options.read-by-index: Reaching clue 50, because the links lead straight to it
options.read-every-clue: Reading out every clue, because each link leads to the next clue

cheaper-on-a-trail.explanation: Adding a stop is cheaper: two link changes on the trail, O(1), while the sheet shifts every clue behind it, O(n). Reaching clue 50 favours the sheet, with O(1) against a walk of 49 links. Reading out every clue costs O(n) on both, because each clue is visited once either way.

linked-list.gloss: A chain of nodes where each node links to the next one and the last links to nothing.

node.gloss: One item of a linked list: a value plus a link to the next node.

head.gloss: The first node of a linked list, where every traversal starts.

pointer.gloss: A labelled marker that refers to one node, like here or prev.

traversal.gloss: Visiting the nodes one after another by following their links.

exercise.title: Run the hunt backwards
exercise.task: Your friends want to run the hunt backwards, from the last clue to the first, so it ends where it began. Write `reverseList`, which takes the [[head]] of the [[linked-list]] and returns the new head after reversing it in place. Relink the existing [[node]] objects instead of building a new trail, and handle an empty hunt too.
hints: You need to remember the clue before the current one, because a node has no link back to it.
At each step, save `next` before you change any link, or you lose the rest of the hunt.
Walk with `prev` set to `null` and `current` set to `head`. Flip `current.next` to `prev`, then move both forward. When `current` is `null`, `prev` is the new head.
